questions.text: Why do very deep plain CNNs (without skip connections) sometimes show higher training error than shallower CNNs?
options: The increased capacity leads to severe overfitting on the training set before convergence can be reached.
Optimization becomes harder; skip connections make learning identity mappings easier and improve gradient flow.
The receptive field becomes excessively large, causing the network to lose fine-grained spatial information.
Saturated activations cause exploding gradients that cannot be mitigated by standard initialization techniques.
questions.correct_answer: Optimization becomes harder; skip connections make learning identity mappings easier and improve gradient flow.

questions.text: In a standard ResNet-50 bottleneck block, the three convolutions are typically:
In Inception/GoogLeNet modules, the main purpose of 1×1 convolutions is to:
options: Increase the receptive field of subsequent convolutional layers without downsampling.
Reduce channel dimensionality (bottleneck) and add non-linearity
Act as a differentiable substitute for max-pooling operations to preserve exact spatial hierarchies.
Project the feature maps into a higher-dimensional space to separate entangled features.
questions.correct_answer: Reduce channel dimensionality (bottleneck) and add non-linearity

questions.text: MobileNetV1 reduces computation primarily by using:
options: Grouped convolutions followed by spatial pyramid pooling
Depthwise separable convolutions (depthwise + pointwise)
Asymmetric convolutions (e.g., factorizing a 3×3 into 3×1 followed by 1×3)
Low-rank matrix factorization of dense classification layers

questions.text: EfficientNet’s key scaling idea is:
options: Scaling the network depth logarithmically while linearly increasing the input resolution
Utilizing neural architecture search (NAS) to independently optimize depth, width, and resolution for each block
Compound scaling of depth, width, and resolution using a single coefficient
Adjusting the channel multiplier dynamically based on the target device's hardware constraints
questions.correct_answer: Compound scaling of depth, width, and resolution using a single coefficient

questions.text: You have a pretrained CNN backbone and only 500 labeled images for a new task. A strong first baseline is:
options: Fine-tune the entire network immediately using a very small learning rate to preserve pre-trained features
Freeze backbone, train a new classifier head; optionally unfreeze later with smaller LR
Train a completely new architecture from scratch using heavy data augmentation to compensate for the lack of data
Unfreeze the backbone from the bottom layers upwards, gradually increasing the learning rate
questions.correct_answer: Freeze backbone, train a new classifier head; optionally unfreeze later with smaller LR

questions.text: When fine-tuning a model, what is a common way to prevent the new training from "overwriting" or destroying the useful features already learned during pre-training?
options: Applying a high dropout rate exclusively to the newly initialized classification head
Use differential learning rates (small LR for the pre-trained backbone, larger LR for the new head)
Re-initializing the weights of the last convolutional block before training
Freezing the classification head and only fine-tuning the backbone features
questions.correct_answer: Use differential learning rates (small LR for the pre-trained backbone, larger LR for the new head)

Grad-CAM

questions.text: Which detector is a classic two-stage detector with an RPN + ROI feature extraction?
options: SSD
YOLO

questions.text: Which statement is most accurate?
options: Two-stage detectors optimize a single joint loss function for classification and localization, whereas single-stage uses decoupled losses.
Single-stage detectors rely on selective search for region generation, whereas two-stage detectors use a dedicated sub-network.
Two-stage detectors typically generate proposals then classify/refine; single- stage predicts boxes/classes densely.
Two-stage detectors process the entire image in one pass, while single-stage detectors evaluate crops sequentially.
questions.correct_answer: Two-stage detectors typically generate proposals then classify/refine; single- stage predicts boxes/classes densely.

questions.text: RetinaNet is notable primarily because it introduced:
options: A novel feature pyramid network (FPN) architecture that eliminates the need for anchor boxes
Focal loss to address class imbalance
The concept of Region of Interest (RoI) pooling to align features extracted from different scales
A dynamic routing mechanism that directly assigns bounding box predictions to ground truth objects
questions.correct_answer: Focal loss to address class imbalance

questions.text: A model that predicts a class label for every pixel without separating object instances is:
options: Panoptic segmentation
Instance segmentation
Semantic segmentation
Image matting

questions.text: Vanishing gradients in vanilla RNNs are largely caused by:
options: The continuous addition of bias terms at each timestep which suppresses the gradient signal
Repeated multiplication by Jacobians whose spectral norm is often < 1
The use of unbounded activation functions like ReLU that cause activations to decay over time
The inability of the standard cross-entropy loss function to distinguish between short-term and long-term dependencies
questions.correct_answer: Repeated multiplication by Jacobians whose spectral norm is often < 1

questions.text: Which statement is true?
options: Transformers process sequences sequentially but utilize parallelized loss computation to speed up training.
The attention mechanism strictly limits the context window size, whereas RNNs have a theoretically infinite context window in practice.
Self-attention enables direct interactions between any pair of tokens within a layer.
Transformers inherently encode positional information in their feed-forward weights, eliminating the need for explicit sequence tracking.
questions.correct_answer: Self-attention enables direct interactions between any pair of tokens within a layer.

questions.text: Which statements can be true in practice when fine-tuning with small batch sizes?
options: Freezing BatchNorm running statistics can improve stability.
If the new dataset distribution differs, re-estimating BN stats may help.
Setting BatchNorm to training mode with a batch size of 1 provides an unbiased estimate of the population variance.
Calling .eval() on a BatchNorm layer disables the application of the learned affine parameters (γ, β).
correct_answer: Freezing BatchNorm running statistics can improve stability.
If the new dataset distribution differs, re-estimating BN stats may help.

questions.text: Which statements are true?
options: Smooth L1 (Huber) is often used for box regression due to robustness to outliers.
Focal loss primarily addresses foreground/background (class) imbalance.
Standard Cross-Entropy loss scales the loss of easy examples to zero more aggressively than Focal Loss.
In two-stage detectors, the RPN has its own objectness + box regression losses.
correct_answer: Smooth L1 (Huber) is often used for box regression due to robustness to outliers.
Focal loss primarily addresses foreground/background (class) imbalance.
In two-stage detectors, the RPN has its own objectness + box regression losses.

questions.text: Which statements are true ?
options: Soft attention is differentiable and can be trained with backpropagation.
Hard attention often needs sampling + REINFORCE (or similar) due to non- differentiability.
Soft attention significantly reduces the computational complexity of the forward pass compared to Hard attention.
Cross-attention can align decoder queries to encoder keys/values (e.g., words attending to image regions).
correct_answer: Soft attention is differentiable and can be trained with backpropagation.
Hard attention often needs sampling + REINFORCE (or similar) due to non- differentiability.
Cross-attention can align decoder queries to encoder keys/values (e.g., words attending to image regions).
